findings.description: The RDS instance sets storage_encrypted = false, so the database files, automated backups, read replicas, and snapshots are stored unencrypted. Anyone obtaining access to the underlying storage or a snapshot can read the application data directly.

publicly_accessible = true assigns the RDS instance a public IP so it can be reached from the internet. Combined with the predictable identifier and static admin credentials, this greatly enlarges the attack surface for brute-force and exploitation.

The master username is the fixed value "admin" rather than a unique, non-guessable account name. Default administrative account names are the first target of credential-stuffing and brute-force attempts.

The master password is supplied as var.password and stored in state/configuration in plain text, and the lifecycle block explicitly ignores changes to it. Treating a committed or state-resident secret as acceptable means the credential must be considered compromised and cannot be rotated cleanly.

backup_retention_period = 0 disables automated backups and point-in-time recovery. This is primarily a resilience control, but it also removes the ability to recover data after a destructive compromise; noted for completeness as a weak security posture rather than an exploitable misconfiguration.

The database password (and endpoint, username, and database name) is interpolated directly into the EC2 user_data script and written to /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc in world-readable web content. Anyone with ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute, and any process on the instance or path traversal in the web server, can read the database credential.

No metadata_options block is present, so the instance uses the default IMDS configuration that permits unauthenticated credential retrieval over IMDSv1. A server-side request forgery in the deployed PHP application turns into theft of the instance profile credentials.

The startup script writes the DB password into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc and serves the PHP application from Apache, placing credentials in the web content tree. Exposure of that file exposes the database directly.

The policy grants s3:*, ec2:*, and rds:* on Resource "*", which is effectively administrative access over storage, compute, and databases. Compromise of the EC2 instance or its credentials yields full control of those services in the account, far beyond what the catalog application needs.

MySQL port 3306 is opened to the entire VPC CIDR rather than to the specific application security group. Every instance in the VPC, including unrelated or compromised workloads, can reach the database; the rule should reference the application's security group instead of the whole VPC range.

The egress rule allows all protocols, all ports, to 0.0.0.0/0. The database security group has no reason to initiate arbitrary outbound connections, and this provides a data-exfiltration and command-and-control channel for a compromised or misused database instance.

The MySQL parameter group does not enforce TLS for connections (for example via require_secure_transport), so clients may connect to the database without encryption in transit. Credentials and query data can be transmitted in cleartext on the network.

The AMI filter searches for an image named "amzn2-ami-hvm-*-x86_64-portal-disk" while owners is restricted to "amazon". If no Amazon-owned AMI matches this non-standard name, resolution can fail or, if it matches an image published under a differently controlled account, deploy an unverified image. The filter should pin a known-good, verifiable AMI rather than a wildcard name.
